claims.claim: A presentation is a prepared talk that gives information about something to an audience.

Presentations differ from everyday conversation: one speaker carries the message to many listeners at once, the content is organized in advance, and listeners do not trade turns as they do in conversation.
An effective opening engages the audience with a hook, such as a question, and organizes the talk so the audience can follow what comes next.
A well-organized presentation sticks to a few main points, and logical organization helps both the speaker and the audience follow along.
A strong closing restates the main points and ends with the most important takeaway the speaker wants the audience to remember.
Visuals such as slides should support the speaker rather than replace them; slides with too much text or too many effects pull the audience's attention away from the speech.
Rehearsing aloud and recording yourself reduce filler words and build confidence before a presentation.
A rhetorical question is a question asked in order to make a point, not to receive an answer.
During the question period, if a speaker did not hear part of a question, it is normal to politely ask the listener to repeat it.
Oral communication has both verbal and nonverbal dimensions: tone of voice, facial expression, and body language carry meaning alongside the words.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How much text belongs on a slide
positions: Some presenters use detailed slides as speaking notes or as a record the audience can keep
Purdue OWL advises using the PowerPoint as an aid to the presentation, not as the presentation, and favors as little text as possible
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the general principle that slides support the speaker with brief keywords and images and that detailed material belongs in a handout; it makes no claim about a specific word count.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether to memorize a script or speak from notes
positions: Memorizing word for word can feel safe but leaves a speaker lost if a single line is forgotten
Purdue OWL advises treating yourself as a mini-expert on the topic rather than simply memorizing slide or note-card content
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson recommends learning the structure and key points, rehearsing aloud, and recording yourself, without prescribing one delivery style.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Which signposting phrases a speaker must use
positions: Teaching materials often present a standard set of signposting phrases such as first, next, finally, and in conclusion
Real speech varies with context, register, and personal style
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents signposting phrases as a starter toolkit with original examples, not as a fixed script, and keeps the guidance general.

sourceRecords.title: Public Speaking and Presentations: Tips for Success
sourceRecords.provider: Purdue Online Writing Lab (OWL), Purdue University
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (Purdue OWL is a named Tier A source in the subject source map). Read live on 2026-08-21 (HTTP 200): the page and its linked handout document public-speaking-updated-20250731.docx. Supports: adapting delivery to the audience; sticking to a few main points with logical organization that helps the audience follow; opening with a hook such as a question; summarizing the main points and ending with the most important takeaway; visual aids that do not distract from the speech; rehearsing to reduce filler words and recording yourself; relaxing; preparing extra examples and details to stay calm during Q&A. Reference only; prose synthesized.

sourceRecords.provider: Purdue Online Writing Lab (OWL), Purdue University
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. sourceRecords.title: presentation — Cambridge Dictionary
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B. Read live on 2026-08-21 (HTTP 200). Defines a presentation as 'a talk giving information about something', with the example 'The speaker gave an interesting presentation on urban transport.' Supports the core definition of the topic and the one-to-many, information-giving framing.

sourceRecords.title: audience — Cambridge Dictionary
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B. Read live on 2026-08-21 (HTTP 200). Defines an audience as the group of people together in one place to watch or listen to someone speaking. Supports the vocabulary entry and the one-to-many framing of presentations.

sourceRecords.title: rhetorical question — Cambridge Dictionary
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B. Read live on 2026-08-21 (HTTP 200). Defines a rhetorical question as 'a question, asked in order to make a statement, that does not expect an answer'. Supports the audience-engagement content and the vocabulary entry.

sourceRecords.title: pardon — Cambridge Dictionary
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B. Read live on 2026-08-21 (HTTP 200). The entry states that 'pardon' is said when you have not heard what someone has said and you want the person to repeat it, and that 'pardon me' politely asks someone to repeat something said because you did not hear it. Supports the Q&A strategy of asking a listener for repetition.

sourceRecords.title: Business English for Success, Section 9.1 Oral versus Written Communication
sourceRecords.notes: Read live on 2026-08-21 (HTTP 200). Supports: face-to-face oral communication gives immediate feedback while written communication is asynchronous; oral communication has verbal and nonverbal dimensions (tone of voice, facial expression, body language). Used only for the conversation-versus-presentation contrast framing (immediacy of feedback, prepared vs. spontaneous). License text was not visible in the copies read; used as reference only.
